title: Rebase vs Merge
summary: Rebase rewrites history instead of combining it — replaying your commits onto a new base with brand-new hashes. Learn what that buys you, why it's dangerous on shared branches, and when merge is the safer default.

slides.markdown:
[Merging](branching-merging) combines two histories by adding a new commit that has two parents. **Rebasing** takes the opposite approach: it removes your branch's commits, then replays them one by one on top of a different starting point, as if you'd written them there all along.

The result looks cleaner — a straight line instead of a fork-and-rejoin shape — but the mechanism is fundamentally more invasive: every replayed commit gets a **new hash**, because a commit's hash includes its parent. Rebase doesn't move commits, it recreates them.

That one fact is the source of both rebase's biggest benefit (linear, readable history) and its biggest danger (rewriting commits other people already have a copy of). This topic is about knowing which situation you're in before you run it.

slides.subTitle: Replay, don't reconcile
slides.markdown:
`git rebase main` while standing on `feature` does three things in sequence:

1. Finds the commits on `feature` that aren't on `main` (everything since their merge base).
2. Temporarily sets them aside.
3. Moves `feature`'s pointer to `main`'s current tip, then re-applies each set-aside commit one at a time, as a brand-new commit, on top of that tip.

Each new commit has the same author, message, and diff as the original — but a **different parent**, which means a **different hash**. The old commits still exist in git's object database for a while (findable via the reflog), but `feature` no longer points to them; it points to the new, rebased chain.

This is why rebase is described as *rewriting* history rather than *combining* it: nothing about `main` changes, and `feature` ends up with commits that never existed before the rebase ran.

slides.sectionTitle: The same two branches, merged vs rebased
slides.markdown:
Take identical starting branches — `main` with two commits since the fork, `feature` with three — and look at the resulting shape under each operation.

**Merged:** both branches' commits stay exactly as they were, plus one new merge commit with two parents joining them. The fork is visible forever in `git log --graph`.

**Rebased:** `feature`'s three commits are recreated with new hashes directly on top of `main`'s tip. There's no fork, no merge commit — just one straight line, as if `feature` had been built starting from where `main` currently is.

Both end up with the same final file contents. What differs is entirely the **shape of the history** left behind, and — critically — every commit hash on the rebased `feature` is now different from what it was before, which matters the moment anyone else already has a copy of the old ones.

slides.subTitle: pick / reword / squash / fixup / drop
slides.markdown:
`git rebase -i main` opens an editable list of your branch's commits, oldest first, each prefixed with an action:

```
pick a1b2c3d Add rate limiter middleware
pick e4f5g6h Fix typo in rate limiter comment
pick h7i8j9k WIP debugging
squash k1l2m3n Actually fix the rate limiter bug
```

Changing the leading word changes what happens to that commit when the rebase replays it:

```
reword  — keep the commit, edit its message
squash  — merge this commit into the one above, keep both messages
fixup   — merge into the one above, discard this commit's message entirely
drop    — remove the commit from history completely
```

This is the standard way to clean up a feature branch before opening a PR: fold "fix typo" and "WIP debugging" commits into the real change they belong to, so the PR's history tells a clean story instead of an exact diary of how you got there.

slides.subTitle: Never rebase commits others have already pulled
slides.markdown:
Because rebase gives every replayed commit a new hash, rebasing a branch that someone else has already fetched creates two divergent, unrelated-looking histories for what used to be the same commits — theirs still point at the old hashes, yours now points at new ones with identical content but no shared identity.

The rule that avoids this entirely: **only rebase commits that exist solely on your own branch, that nobody else has fetched or based work on.** Your own in-progress feature branch, before you've shared it — completely safe to rebase freely. A shared `main` or `develop` that other people pull from daily — never rebase it.

The grey area is a pushed-but-still-personal feature branch: safe to rebase if you're the only one using it, dangerous the moment a teammate has checked it out or a CI system has cached its old commits for a long-running job. When in doubt, ask before rewriting a branch's history that isn't purely yours.

A rebase replays commits one at a time, so a conflict can happen on any single commit in the sequence — not just once, the way a merge conflict does:

```bash
$ git rebase main
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in api.py
error: could not apply e4f5g6h... Fix rate limiter edge case
```

At this point you're mid-rebase with three options:

```bash
# fix the conflict markers in the file, then:
git add api.py
git rebase --continue      # apply this commit, move to the next one

git rebase --skip          # abandon this one commit entirely, keep going

git rebase --abort         # undo the whole rebase, back to how you started
```

`--continue` repeats for every subsequent commit that conflicts — a rebase of ten commits can, in the worst case, mean resolving the same underlying conflict ten times if an early commit introduced a change every later commit touches. `--abort` is always safe: it fully restores the branch to its pre-rebase state.

slides.subTitle: Readable line vs preserved truth
slides.markdown:
| | Rebase | Merge |
|---|---|---|
| History shape | Linear, no forks | Forks and rejoins, true shape preserved |
| Commit hashes | Rewritten for every replayed commit | Unchanged |
| Safe on shared branches | No — never on commits others have | Yes — always additive, never rewrites |
| Conflict resolution | Potentially once per commit | Once, for the whole merge |
| `git bisect` friendliness | Every commit is a clean, buildable step | Merge commits can hide which side introduced a regression |
| What it optimizes for | A readable, linear story | An honest record of what actually happened |

Neither is strictly better — they optimize for different things. Rebase produces history that reads like it was written in order and bisects cleanly; merge produces history that's honest about the fact that work happened in parallel and never risks rewriting anything. Most teams use both: rebase freely on personal feature branches to clean them up, merge (often via squash) to land them on the shared branch.

slides.sectionTitle: `rebase --onto` for moving to a different base
slides.markdown:
Plain `git rebase main` replays your entire branch onto `main`'s tip. `git rebase --onto` is the more surgical version: it replays only a specific *range* of commits onto a specific *new* base, letting you move part of a branch's history independently.

```bash
git rebase --onto main old-feature-base feature
```

Reads as: "take everything on `feature` since `old-feature-base`, and replay it starting from `main` instead." A concrete use case: you branched `feature-b` off `feature-a` before `feature-a` was reviewed and changed. Once `feature-a` merges, you want `feature-b`'s commits replayed directly onto `main`, skipping `feature-a`'s now-obsolete intermediate commits entirely — `--onto` does exactly that in one command, where a plain rebase would replay `feature-a`'s commits too.

Rebasing changes commit hashes, which means your local branch and the remote's copy now have unrelated-looking histories — a normal `git push` is rejected because it isn't a fast-forward. The fix that makes it work, `git push --force`, is also the fix that silently discards anyone else's work that was pushed to that branch in the meantime.

Concretely: teammate pushes a commit to `shared-feature`. You rebase your local copy and force-push. Their commit is now unreachable from the branch's tip — not merged, not visible in `git log`, effectively gone unless someone finds it via reflog on their own machine, if they even know to look.

The safer default is `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses to force-push if the remote has changed since you last fetched — it fails loudly instead of clobbering silently. Even with that, the underlying rule holds: don't rebase a branch other people are actively pushing to at all.

A plain `git pull` is shorthand for `git fetch` + `git merge` — if your local branch has commits the remote doesn't, pulling creates a merge commit joining them. Do this daily on an active branch and your history fills with small, low-information "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commits.

`git pull --rebase` instead does `git fetch` + `git rebase` — your local commits get replayed on top of the newly-fetched remote tip, with no merge commit at all. History stays linear, at the cost of rewriting your own not-yet-pushed local commits every time you pull (which is safe, precisely because they're only yours).

The golden rule still applies underneath: `pull --rebase` is only rewriting your *local, unpushed* commits, never the remote's. Teams that value a linear log typically set `git config pull.rebase true` globally, so every pull behaves this way without remembering the flag.

slides.subTitle: Same content, different identity
slides.markdown:
Because rebase creates new commits with the same diff but a different hash, git tooling has to work to recognize that two commits are "the same change" after a rebase — and this shows up in real workflows:

- **`git cherry-pick` detection.** If a commit was cherry-picked onto `main` and later the original branch is rebased and merged, git's `-x` flag and patch-id matching can recognize the duplicate change and skip re-applying it — but only if you used the right flags; otherwise you get the same change twice with two different hashes.
- **PR platforms re-request review after a rebase**, even when no line of code actually changed, because every commit's identity changed — this surprises teams that expect "just a rebase" to be invisible to reviewers.
- **`--rebase-merges`** preserves merge commits during a rebase instead of flattening them, useful when a branch intentionally contains sub-merges you don't want linearized away.

The underlying lesson: rebase operates on **commit identity**, not just content, and that distinction leaks into tooling in ways worth anticipating before you run it on anything complex.

Every rebase mistake short of a completed force-push is recoverable, because git doesn't delete the original commits immediately — it just stops pointing at them. `git rebase --abort` undoes an in-progress rebase entirely. Even after a rebase completes, the **reflog** (`git reflog`) still lists the branch's previous position, and `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or the equivalent reflog entry) restores it, as covered in [Undoing Changes & Recovery](undoing-changes-recovery).

The one case that isn't locally recoverable is a completed, pushed, force-pushed rebase that already overwrote a teammate's remote work — at that point recovery depends on someone else's local reflog still having the lost commits, if they ever fetched them. That asymmetry — recoverable locally, potentially unrecoverable once it clobbers someone else's remote — is exactly why the golden rule exists.
